fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I want to separate two things, because people conflate them. There's the question of whether the technology is revolutionary, and there's the question of whether it's a bubble. They're not the same question. You can have a technology that completely changes the world, and you can still have a bubble in it. In fact, the bubbles usually form around the revolutionary technologies, because the story is so compelling. In the 1920s you had radio, you had electrification, the automobile. Those changed everything, and the stock market still crashed 89%. In the late nineties the internet was going to change the world, and it did, and the Nasdaq still fell about 80%. So the technology being real doesn't protect you from the price being wrong.

So how do I think about it? I've studied every bubble I could find going back a few hundred years, and I have a bubble indicator with about six measures. Let me go through them. First, how high are prices relative to traditional measures of value, like earnings? Second, are prices discounting unsustainable conditions, meaning are the earnings growth rates that are implied by the price rates that have never been sustained over a long period? Third, how many new buyers have entered the market, people who weren't there before? Fourth, how broad is the bullish sentiment? Fifth, how much of the buying is being financed with leverage, with borrowed money? And sixth, are buyers making extended forward purchases, like companies buying a lot of capacity in anticipation of demand? When all of those are high at the same time, you're in a bubble.

Now, if I look at AI today, I'd say we're in the range of maybe 60 to 70 percent of the way to a classic bubble. Prices are high. There's a lot of new buying. Sentiment is very broad. The one thing that's different from 1999 is that the leverage isn't as extreme, and the companies at the center of it are actually very profitable. That matters. But the capital spending is enormous. When you see companies committing hundreds of billions of dollars to build capacity, that's the forward purchasing piece, and that's the piece that historically goes wrong, because the demand comes, but it comes slower than the capacity, and then the margins collapse.

The other thing I'd say is that bubbles don't pop on their own. They pop when money gets tight. So the thing I watch is not whether the technology works. The thing I watch is the amount of liquidity in the system, interest rates, and whether the people who are buying are buying with money they have or money they borrowed. The technology is the story, but the mechanics of the bubble are always about money and credit.

And then the last point, which is the most important one for an investor. Even if the technology wins, that doesn't tell you which companies win. In the automobile era, there were hundreds of car companies and nearly all of them went bankrupt. The internet won and most internet companies died. So the question isn't "is AI real?" Of course it's real. The question is "what's priced in, who's going to capture the value, and what happens when the money gets tighter?" If you think about it that way, you're thinking about it like an investor rather than like someone caught up in the story.

r001.rationale: It explains that a compelling story around revolutionary technology can fuel a bubble and lead to prices being wrong, even when the technology is real.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says a technology can change the world while its investments are overpriced, citing the internet and other technologies as examples.

r003.rationale: It lists high prices relative to earnings and unsustainable implied growth as bubble measures, but identifies tighter money and capacity outpacing demand as reversal mechanics—not profits failing to justify stock prices as a trigger.

opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that you have to separate two things that people tend to confuse: whether the technology is real, and whether the investment is good. Those are very different. I have no doubt that AI is a revolutionary technology, maybe the most important of my lifetime. It's going to change productivity, the way we work, the way we learn, almost everything. But history shows that great technologies very often produce bad investments, because people get so excited that they pay too much.

Look at the railroads, the automobile, radio in the 1920s, the internet in the late '90s. In each case the technology delivered, and in each case a lot of the investors who bought at the peak lost most of their money. In 2000 you could have correctly said the internet was going to change the world, and you would have been right. But if you bought those stocks at the top, it took many years, in some cases more than a decade, just to get back to even, and many of those companies didn't survive. So being right about the technology doesn't mean you're going to make money.

The way I think about it, and I've studied a lot of bubbles over hundreds of years, is that they all work roughly the same way. That's why I built what I call a bubble gauge. It looks at a handful of things. Are prices high relative to traditional measures, like earnings? Are prices discounting future growth that would be very hard to achieve? Are there a lot of new, inexperienced buyers coming into the market because they've seen others make money? Is sentiment broadly bullish? Is buying being financed with debt? Are companies and investors making big forward commitments, spending enormous amounts on the expectation that the future is going to be wonderful? When you put those together, you get a sense of how frothy things are.

Right now, if you look at that gauge, we're pretty high up. A lot of the market's gains are concentrated in a small number of companies tied to AI. There are enormous capital expenditures being made on data centers and chips, and more and more of that is being financed with debt. The valuations assume a great deal of future profit. So by my measures, there are a lot of the classic characteristics of a bubble.

But this is the important part. A bubble doesn't burst just because prices are high. People make that mistake. They say, "It's a bubble, so I should get out," and then it keeps going up for a couple of years and they look foolish. Bubbles pop when something forces selling. Usually it's a tightening of money, when interest rates rise or credit gets harder to get, so the people who borrowed to buy have to sell to service their debts. Or it's some need for cash, like taxes or other obligations. Then you get the selling that cracks the market. So I'm less focused on whether it's a bubble and more focused on what could prick it, and watching for that.

I also think you can't look at this in isolation. It's happening at the same time as we have very large government debts, a big wealth gap, a lot of political conflict internally, and geopolitical conflict between great powers, especially the US and China, which is very much a technology war. AI is going to make some people extremely rich and displace a lot of others. If that happens in an environment that's already very divided, you could see political pressure for things like wealth taxes or redistribution, which can be exactly the kind of thing that creates a need for cash and forces selling. So it's all interconnected. It's not just a market question.

So what do I do about it? I don't try to predict the exact top, because nobody does that well. I think about diversification. Don't have all your eggs in the basket that everyone is excited about. Know the difference between the companies that are actually going to capture the profits and the ones that are just riding the excitement, because a lot of the value in a new technology ends up going to the users of it and to society, not necessarily to the companies that built the infrastructure. And be very careful with leverage, because leverage is what turns a decline into a disaster.

So I'm excited about AI as a technology, and I'm cautious about it as an investment. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

r001.rationale: It says excitement about a revolutionary technology can lead investors to pay too much for its investments.

r002.rationale: It explains that technologies such as the internet delivered on their promise while investors who bought at peak prices could lose money.

r003.rationale: It notes that valuations assume substantial future profits, but identifies forced selling from tighter money or cash needs—not profits failing to justify stock prices—as what can trigger a bubble’s reversal.

fable-5.text:
The way I look at it is that there are really two separate questions that people tend to mix together, and mixing them up is where they get into trouble. The first question is: is the technology revolutionary? And the second question is: is the price right? History shows you can answer yes to the first and still lose a tremendous amount of money because of the second.

If you go back and look at history — and I've studied the last five hundred years of these cycles — every great new technology produced this same dynamic. It happened with canals, it happened with railroads, it happened with radio in the 1920s, and it happened with the internet in 2000. The technology was real. It did change the world. But the companies that were bought at bubble prices — many of them still went down eighty, ninety percent, and a lot of them went broke, even though the technology succeeded.

So I have measures of a bubble, and they're pretty mechanical. Are prices high relative to traditional measures of value? Are prices discounting conditions that can't be sustained — in other words, do earnings have to grow at rates that have rarely ever happened to justify them? Are new, naive buyers coming into the market because they feel they're missing out? Is there broad bullish sentiment? And importantly, are purchases being financed by debt and leverage? Because when leverage comes in, that's what turns a decline into a crisis — somebody has to sell to cover, and that selling begets more selling.

When I look at AI today through that lens, I'd say the technology is going to be transformative — I have no doubt about that. It'll raise productivity in ways we can barely imagine. But the pricing in parts of the market is discounting a future that assumes almost nothing goes wrong, and history says something always goes wrong — competition comes in, margins compress, the winners aren't who you expected. In 1929 and in 2000, the problem wasn't that people were wrong about the future. The problem was that they paid prices that assumed the future would arrive on schedule, without disruption, and with the profits going to the particular companies they'd bought.

And you have to see all of this in the context of the bigger picture — the debt cycle, the amount of money and credit in the system. Bubbles don't pop on their own; they pop when the tightening comes, when money gets expensive. So the risk isn't the technology. The risk is the price you pay, the leverage behind it, and where we are in the cycle when the music stops.

r001.rationale: The response says investors can correctly see a technology as revolutionary yet lose money by mixing that judgment with the separate question of price, and describes paying bubble prices despite the technology succeeding.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the technology can change the world while companies bought at bubble prices still fall sharply or go broke.

r003.rationale: It identifies unsustainable earnings growth assumptions as a measure of bubble pricing, but names tightening and expensive money as what pops bubbles; it does not clearly identify profits failing to justify prices as a trigger for reversal.

opus-5.text:
I've studied bubbles going back hundreds of years, and the first thing I'd say is that a bubble and a revolution aren't opposites — they usually come together. Almost every great technology in history arrived with a bubble attached to it. The railroads transformed the world and bankrupted most of the people who financed them. Electricity, the automobile, the radio in the 1920s — all genuinely world-changing, and in each case the companies were priced as though every one of them would be the winner. The internet in 1999 is the clearest modern case. The internet was everything the enthusiasts said it would be. It still wiped out eighty percent of the market value of the companies built on it, because the price already assumed the future. So I never ask myself, "Is this technology real?" That's the wrong question. I ask, "What's discounted in the price?"

I have a bubble indicator I've used for a long time, and it looks at about six things. How high are prices relative to traditional measures of value? Are current conditions being extrapolated far into the future — meaning does the price require a growth rate that has rarely been sustained? Are there new and inexperienced buyers coming into the market? How broad is the bullishness? How much of the buying is being financed with debt? And are people making forward purchases to speculate or hedge against price rises — buying capacity they don't yet need?

When I run that on AI today, I get a mixed reading, and I want to be precise about this. Prices are high. The extrapolation is aggressive — the earnings implied by some of these valuations are extraordinary. Sentiment is very broad; you'd have trouble finding an informed person who'll tell you AI won't matter, and that unanimity is itself a warning sign. What's been somewhat less extreme than in past bubbles, at least until recently, is leverage, because much of this has been funded out of the enormous cash flows of a handful of very profitable companies rather than borrowed. But that's changing. You're now seeing debt-financed data centers, you're seeing circular arrangements where a supplier invests in its own customer who then buys its chips, and that kind of financing structure is exactly what you watch, because it's how a price decline turns into a forced-selling decline.

The other thing I'd add, which people underweight, is that the technology question and the money question are tangled up with a third thing — the debt cycle and the geopolitical cycle. We have enormous government debt needing to be sold, we have internal political conflict, we have a US-China conflict in which these chips are the contested asset. A great technology arriving in a fragile financial and political system doesn't get valued the way it would in a calm one.

So my honest answer: I think AI is probably going to be as transformative as people say, and I think a lot of the capital going into it will be lost, and both of those will be true at the same time. The discipline is to be positioned so that being right about the technology and wrong about the timing doesn't take you out of the game.

r001.rationale: It says revolutionary technologies often come with bubbles, with companies priced as though they would all win, and asks what future is already reflected in the price.

r002.rationale: It says the internet delivered on its promise yet its companies lost 80% of their market value because prices had already assumed that future; it also says AI may be transformative while much of its invested capital is lost.

r003.rationale: It notes that valuations imply extraordinary earnings and that a price decline can cause forced selling, but does not identify profits failing to justify stock prices as a trigger for a bubble’s reversal.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Whenever I think about a bubble, I try not to go on feelings. I look at it systematically. I've studied hundreds of these cases over history, and the pattern is the same each time, so I have a kind of checklist.

First, are prices high relative to traditional measures of value? Second, are those prices dependent on conditions that can't be sustained? Third, how many new buyers have been brought into the market because prices are rising? Fourth, is there broad bullish sentiment, where everyone says it's a sure thing? Fifth, are people buying with leverage, with borrowed money? And sixth, have buyers made extended forward purchases, meaning they are committing to the future because they're convinced the trend will continue?

A revolutionary technology doesn't protect you from a bubble. It makes one more likely. The railroads were transformative, and so were electricity, the automobile, and the internet. Each time, the technology was real and it did change the world, but investors still bid prices far above what the near-term earnings could justify, and a lot of people lost a great deal of money. You can be right about the technology and still be wrong about the investment, because you can pay too much and get the timing wrong.

So with AI, I believe the technology is truly important. It will be a major productivity driver and it will reshape a lot of industries. But I also see some of those bubble characteristics building: very high valuations, a lot of enthusiasm, and a lot of money pouring in. The question is how much of it is financed with debt, and how many people are buying only because the price has gone up.

What I watch most closely is the liquidity. Bubbles don't usually pop because someone decides the technology is a fad. They pop because of tightening, when interest rates rise or the supply of money and credit shrinks, and people who need cash have to sell. Selling then forces more selling. That's the mechanism, and it's why I pay as much attention to the financial conditions around a technology as to the technology itself.

My conclusion is that we're in something that looks like a bubble, but I don't know that it's at the point of bursting. Don't ask only whether AI is real. Ask what's priced in, who's holding it, how they paid for it, and what happens if the money gets tighter.

r001.rationale: It says revolutionary technologies can make bubbles more likely and that investors may bid prices far above near-term earnings even when the technology is real.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the technology can be real and change the world while investors can still pay too much and be wrong about the investment.

r003.rationale: It notes prices can exceed what near-term earnings justify, but attributes bubble reversals to tightening and shrinking money or credit—not to profits failing to justify stock prices.

haiku-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to understand is that a bubble isn't really about the technology. It's about the price people pay for it and how that price is financed. AI is going to change a lot, and that's exactly why people get excited and start extrapolating. The trouble is that excitement moves faster than real productivity gains. Prices rise because people expect the future to arrive quickly, they borrow to buy more, and the borrowing is what makes the whole thing fragile.

When I look at this, I ask a few questions. Is a lot of the buying financed with debt? Are people saying "this time is different" with a straight face? Are valuations far ahead of what the cash flows could plausibly be over the next decade? When all three are flashing, you're in the part of the cycle where the reversal can be painful, even if the technology ends up being enormous.

The internet is a good example. It was transformative, yet many investors who bought in 1999 lost a lot of money. Being right about where the technology goes and being right about the price are two different things. My advice is to hold a view about the long-term direction, but size your positions so you can survive being early or wrong on timing. Diversify, watch the leverage, and remember that a bubble and a real innovation can both be true at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response says excitement about AI’s transformative potential leads investors to extrapolate and push prices ahead of real productivity gains.

r002.rationale: It says the internet was transformative even though many investors who bought in 1999 lost money, and that a bubble and real innovation can coexist.

r003.rationale: It identifies valuations far ahead of plausible cash flows as one of the warning signs and says a painful reversal can follow when those signs are present.

astra-6.text:
Well, I would separate two questions: Is this technology going to change the world? And is the price you’re paying for an investment justified? Those are very different questions. You can be right about the technology and still lose money on the investment.

When people see something revolutionary, there’s a tendency to extrapolate—to imagine enormous growth and become less sensitive to price. But the price already contains expectations. So the question is: What does this company actually have to earn to justify that price? And how likely is it to capture those earnings when everybody else is competing for them?

Then I would look at how those investments are financed. If there’s a lot of borrowing, a disappointment can become forced selling. That’s what can turn a decline into something much more damaging.

So enthusiasm about AI, by itself, doesn’t tell you whether there’s a bubble. You have to examine the expectations embedded in prices and the vulnerability of the people holding those investments. Something can be extraordinary and still be too expensive.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think you have to separate the technology from the investment. AI could be revolutionary, and you could still pay too much for it. Those two things can both be true.

When you buy an investment, you’re buying future cash flows. So the question is: what does the price already assume? Does it assume enormous growth? Does it assume that this particular company will capture the profits? And how much room is there for things to turn out differently?

With a revolutionary technology, there’s tremendous uncertainty about who the winners will be. Something can be enormously valuable to society without all of that value becoming profits for the companies supplying it. Competition matters. The cost of building it matters.

Then I’d look at what’s financing the buying. If prices rise, people become more enthusiastic, and they borrow to buy more, you get a reinforcing process. But that process can work in reverse. If expectations disappoint and people have to sell to meet their obligations, the decline becomes much more dangerous.

So I wouldn’t ask only, ‘Is AI going to change the world?’ I’d ask, ‘What am I paying, what has to happen to justify that price, and can I survive being wrong?’ You don’t have to dismiss the technology to be careful about the investment.

terra-5.6.text:
The first thing is to distinguish between the technology and the investment. A technology can be revolutionary and still be a bad investment if you pay too much for it. We saw that with the internet: the internet changed the world, but many of the companies people bought at peak prices were poor investments.

So I look at bubbles as periods when people are extrapolating the recent past far into the future, when prices discount almost perfect outcomes, and when there is a lot of leverage and speculation. AI will produce enormous changes, but the question for an investor is: what is already priced in, who will capture the profits, and what could disappoint?

The sensible approach is diversification and humility. You want exposure to the upside, because you don't want to miss a major paradigm shift, but you don't want to bet your future on the assumption that you know exactly how it will unfold.

sol-5.6.text: I’d separate the technology from the investment. You look at how quickly prices are rising, how much leverage and speculation are involved, whether buyers are focused on cash flows or simply expecting to sell to someone else at a higher price, and how dependent the boom is on easy money. The difficult part is that a bubble doesn’t mean the underlying idea is wrong—it often means people are right about the transformation but wrong about the timing, the winners, or the price they should pay.
